item.title: July 2026 Plays
item.description:
Hello everyone!

July was a good month, full of nice surprises. Lots of sun, beach, and also work 😅, but plenty of fun too, along with some lovely discoveries. Looking back at what I said I’d play last month, I managed everything: getting Black Rose Wars: Rebirth to the table, finishing the It’s a Wonderful World Leisure & Decadence campaign, and playing my first 50 Clues escape game. So let’s take a look at how July went.

July 2026 by Numbers

  • 20 plays (vs. 22 in June)
  • 12 different games
  • 7 new games to me
  • Most played: It’s a Wonderful World
  • Solo plays: 20 (all)

New Games

Earth

Designed by Maxime Tardif, published by Inside Up Games.

In Earth, you’re growing your own ecosystem in a tableau-building game, aiming to build the best one on the table. You’ll score by completing common and personal objectives and by scoring the points on your own cards, and being first to complete a common objective earns you even more. The game is beautiful: the illustrations taught me things about flora I didn’t know, and every card carries a little flavour text that enriches the experience.

I’ve only played solo twice so far, and I’ll definitely be playing more, I loved it. There are no dead moments: when you select an action, all other players (including the automa) get to act too as a result of your choice, so you benefit from everyone else’s decisions along the way. The automa itself is lovely to run, just a simple stack of cards that tells you what it does and which cards you can activate on your own tableau. Where you place your cards matters too, since you activate them left to right, top to bottom, so setting up a benefit early can help unlock an action on a later card. That’s the piece that made me fall in love with the game.

It took me a while to try it, it had a huge hype around it, and the photos alone didn’t pull me in. I was so wrong. Once you play it, you see how beautiful it really is and how everything clicks into place. For now it’s a solid 9/10 for me, though that could change with more plays.

Race for the Galaxy

Designed by Thomas Lehmann, published by Rio Grande Games.

Race for the Galaxy is a galactic civilisation game played entirely with cards, and it plays like a real race: the moment any player has deployed 12 cards, the game ends. I’ve only played it solo so far, and I didn’t expect to love it as much as I do. I originally got the game through a mystery box, and since I didn’t own the expansion at the time, it wasn’t solo playable. I later picked up the Expansion and Brinkmanship set after someone told me it was really good, and I’m glad I did. Beyond the extra cards, this set is also what brings the solo mode, along with three expansion decks. I haven’t opened any of those decks yet, so far I’ve only used the automa, which is simply a small board and two dice.

The game has a clever mechanic that keeps dead moments away: each player secretly selects the action they want to play, then everyone reveals simultaneously, and all players resolve every action chosen. Your own selected action comes with a bonus, while everyone else’s version of that action stays basic. Solo, you choose your two actions upfront and then roll the two automa dice to see what it does, a mechanic that can either launch your strategy forward or leave you unable to act because you’re short on resources. And speaking of resources, there aren’t any separate from the cards, cards are your money and your resources both, which I love.

I’ve played it once in July, plus once more already in August, and found it interesting and challenging. I want to explore this game a lot more, and I’d like to try it at a higher player count to see how it holds up. For now it’s an 8.5/10, but that could change with more plays.

Black Rose Wars: Rebirth

Designed by Andrea Colletti, Diego Fonseca, and Marco Montanaro, published by Ludus Magnus Studio.

Black Rose Wars: Rebirth is a game of planning and strategy, where you compete in a tournament at the Lodge against other mages. It combines deckbuilding with careful planning, all set in a dark magic world. Each turn you select the cards you want to play and lay them on your player board in the order they’ll resolve. Every card actually holds two different actions on the same face, printed upside down from each other, so which one you get depends on which way up you place the card. The actions themselves are usually things like summoning demons, activating them, fighting and dealing damage to other mages, or rebuilding rooms, along with a few other effects. Beyond the cards, you also get two extra actions each turn that you can use whenever you like: moving and activating a room, fighting, or activating a demon.

At solo, you play against an avatar, the base game comes with one, and more are available through expansions. I own the Rotas Box and the Jukas avatar, so one of my plays was against the base game’s avatar and the other against Jukas. I really enjoyed both plays and liked the solo experience. I can see this being fantastic at 3 or 4 players thanks to the interactivity, but even solo the avatar is so well designed that you can feel that interaction come through. It’s both a challenge and a pleasure to play, I love the theme, the art, how the game shines on the table, and the miniatures that bring the theme perfectly to life.

I’ll be playing more, since I still want to explore the rest of the Rotas Box content, there’s a lot in there. I’d recommend this to anyone who loves a mage theme. For now it’s an 8.5/10.

Preferred Game of the Month

It’s a Wonderful World

Designed by Frédéric Guérard, published by La Boîte de Jeu.

This game hardly needs another introduction on my blog, I’ve already said it’s a 10/10 for me, and you can read my full review here. I’ve finally finished the Leisure & Decadence campaign, and I’m in love. This expansion is the best of the three, and it brings a whole new dimension to the game. I don’t want to spoil it, so I won’t say more, but if you love this game already, play the campaign, you’ll love it even more.

Other Notable Games

More New Games

Cyberion (designed by Shadi Torbey, published by inPatience) — Cyberion is part of the Oniverse world, where you’re in charge of maintaining the dream factory. The game centres on a board where you track the upgrades you purchase for each colour of action card. I’ve played it once so far and enjoyed the brain-teaser at its heart: each turn you discard cards from your display to fulfil a machine’s requirements, and you must repair at least one machine every turn or lose the game. It’s fun and keeps you thinking about how to find a solution. I’ll rate it 7/10 for now, it’s enjoyable, though I still prefer Onirim or Nautilion.

Tiny Epic Crimes (designed by Scott Almes, published by Gamelyn Games) — Tiny Epic Crimes is a deduction game where you play a detective trying to identify the criminal. At the start you seal a card of the culprit inside an envelope, and you have several characteristics to work with to help narrow down who it is. Through the game you’ll solve situations and put criminals behind bars, all of which helps you gather more clues toward your deduction. It has some real Cluedo vibes, which brought back some nice nostalgia. My own play didn’t go so well, I felt like I ran out of time to solve the crime, probably because I hadn’t optimised my actions yet. I’ll need a few more plays to fully enjoy it. So far it’s a 6/10 for me, but that could go up.

Ugly Gryphon Inn (designed by Scott Almes, published by Button Shy Games) — Ugly Gryphon Inn is a micro game, just a small deck of cards, where you run the Gryphon Inn and place arriving guests into rooms. Be careful with each guest’s specific requests: if one doesn’t want to be next to another, say, because of a dislike for beer drinkers, it triggers an effect, sometimes making them leave, and sometimes that departure sets off a chain reaction that empties out the inn and loses you the game. It’s a smart little puzzle, and of the Button Shy games I own, it’s the one I like best. I’ll give it an 8/10.

50 Clues: Dead or Alive (designed by Jeppe Norsker, published by Norsker Games) — 50 Clues: Dead or Alive is a crime-solving game where you follow clues through cards to solve a mystery, a murder in this case. You’ll need internet access, since a website walks you through solving the puzzles. I played this one solo, on a day I was tired, which turned out to be a bad combination for this kind of game, and I was pretty bad at solving the puzzles. Since I was so tired, I honestly can’t say whether that was on me or whether the puzzles were genuinely tricky. I won’t give it a rating yet, I still have two more games left in this trilogy, and I’ll have a better sense of it once I’ve finished.

Returning Favourites

Harry Potter: Hogwarts Battle (designed by Forrest-Pruzan Creative, Kami Mandell, and Andrew Wolf, published by The Op) — This will be my next review, so I won’t say too much yet, but I love this game. It’s not always the mechanically best game that you enjoy the most, and as a Potter fan, this one just makes sense for me. Over the years I’ve played it solo, at two players, and at four, and loved it at every count, though this month it was solo only. I’ve already played the Monster Box expansion and I’m curious to try Charms & Potions next, so expect more on that soon. 7/10, and you’ll understand why once the full review is up.

Era of Kingdoms (designed by Michael Erisman, published by KC Games) — You develop your kingdom, bringing it from darkness into light. I recently reviewed this one and rated it 7/10, it’s a deck-building game that’s easy to start and genuinely enjoyable, a nice one for new players and a good discovery for me. Just one play this month, but I’ll be back for more.

Numbsters (designed by Milan Zivkovic, published by Button Shy Games) — A small game, perfect for travel, with lovely illustrations that lean a little toward a kids’-book style. You’re aiming to end with only two cards in hand, the 8 and one other, since around the 8 the smallest number in a sequence eats the biggest, and you can also trigger effects from the top card. I’ve read there’s a way to always win because the game is technically broken, but I haven’t figured it out and I lose often! I still really enjoy picking it up without overthinking it. 7/10, not perfect, but perfect for a quick 10-minute game.

ROVE: Results-Oriented Versatile Explorer (designed by Dustin Dobson and Milan Zivkovic, published by Button Shy Games) — Another Button Shy favourite, this time a programming and movement game where you’re a little robot exploring space. To solve a card, you place your cards to match the exact pattern shown in the image, discarding cards for movement points and moving based on each card’s characteristics. It’s an enjoyable little challenge that travels well, I bring it along wherever I go.

Looking Ahead

For August, I’m hoping to get more Black Rose Wars: Rebirth to the table with some of the Rotas Box content, and to try Dune: Imperium and Coming of Age, both new to me. I’m really excited to give them a go.

What About You?

And you, what did you play this month? I’d love to hear your thoughts! Come find me on Mastodon and Facebook.

item.title: Rise of a Kingdom: My Time with Era of Kingdoms
item.description:
Hello everyone!

Today I’m taking you to the Era of Kingdoms, where you’ll build your domain, attract people to it, and go head to head with rival kingdoms. Who will come out on top as the strongest realm? Let’s find out how to play!

Game Overview

Era of Kingdoms is a 2019 release for 1 to 4 players, ages 14+, with a playtime of 30 to 45 minutes. It was designed by Michael Erisman and illustrated by Jeff Porter and published by KC Games.

Theme

In Era of Kingdoms, you compete to bring your kingdom from the dark ages into the age of enlightenment. You’ll cultivate your lands, build up your military strength and defences, and strike up trades along the way. You’ll also attract people to populate your lands and help carry you to victory.

Gameplay

The rules are simple. The game is played in turns, and each turn gives you 3 actions to spend. You can use them to play a card from your hand, draw a basic card from the deck, or draft a basic card from the Trade Route board if you’re using that expansion. On top of that, at no action cost and with no limit, you can remove cards from your board (except plague cards) and use a Riches card to borrow resources from another player, once per turn.

Every card has resource requirements it needs met before it can be played, drawn from the lands and people already in your kingdom. Once you have 3 level 2 cards in play, you place your town centre card to show your kingdom is growing. Get 3 level 3 cards on the table and you can flip your card over to the castle side, the highest kingdom level there is.

Upgrading is genuinely worth chasing, not just for show. Once you reach town centre level, you can draw or draft 1 card from the intermediate deck each turn on top of your basic cards. Reach castle level and you can draw or draft 1 advanced card and 2 intermediate cards each turn. This is where the game really opens up, since better cards mean better options.

The game ends when the Age of Enlightenment card appears, which happens once players start drawing from the advanced deck. Whoever draws it gets one final point, and everyone gets one last turn to grab as many Victory Points as they can before scores are tallied.

How to Win

The winner is whoever ends the game with the most Victory Points. You earn these mainly through era 2 and era 3 cards, which can be land cards, people cards, or “Play Immediately” cards. The Age of Enlightenment card, which signals the last turn of the game, also gives one point to whoever draws it.

Components

The game is packed with cards, along with a handful of boards. You’ll find components for the base game plus all 3 mini expansions inside the box, with no tokens to speak of. The card quality is good, and the illustrations are beautiful and thematic throughout. The boards match that same quality, nicely illustrated too.

The box cover fits the theme with its dark colours echoing that journey from the dark ages to enlightenment, but it’s also a bit faded, which means it can easily get lost on a shelf next to other games. The rulebook, on the other hand, is well explained, with a good typography size that’s easy to read without straining.

Setup

Setup is quick. Shuffle the 3 card decks (basic, intermediate, and advanced), then place the Enlightenment card at a set position from the top: 9 cards for a 2 player game, 11 for 3 players, or 13 for 4 players. Each player sets up their own board with 3 Riches cards, 1 town centre card, and 1 player turn guide, then draws 5 basic cards.

If you’re already familiar with deck builders, I’d recommend adding the Trade Route expansion straight away, solo or multiplayer. This adds a river of cards: for setup, place 6 basic cards, 3 intermediate, and 1 advanced face up on the Trade Route board.

Solo Mode

The solo opponent, the Shadow Kingdom, is refreshingly easy to manage. Each turn, the Shadow Kingdom draws cards based on your own kingdom’s progression, not its own, so the better you’re doing, the more it draws too. These cards go straight into its play area. At the end of the game, you total up both scores and compare. The trick is staying attentive to what the Shadow Kingdom is collecting, so you can try to optimise your own cards along the way.

My Experience

I’ve played Era of Kingdoms solo 3 times so far. My first game was the pure base game, and the next two included the Trade Route mini expansion, which for me is a must have.

  • Game 1: 21 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 31 (Shadow Kingdom won)
  • Game 2: 27 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 14 (I won!)
  • Game 3: 26 vs the Shadow Kingdom’s 32 (Shadow Kingdom won)

One thing that stood out in my first game was having a good people card in hand but my person tiles already full. In that moment I had to decide whether the new card was worth discarding an existing one for, or whether I was better off sticking with what I had. The start of the game can also be a bit tricky solo, since you sometimes need a specific land card to build on and it can be hard to find in the deck. Luckily the basic deck has a lot of duplicates, so it’s not too bad, but you can still struggle a little, and changing direction isn’t always possible depending on what’s in your hand.

As for the Trade Route expansion, playing without it didn’t feel like real deck building to me, since there’s no card river. You’re stuck with whatever random cards you draw, with no control at all. That’s fine for newer players, but for anyone with more deck building experience under their belt, it’s not quite satisfying enough. Adding the Trade Route brings back that deck building feel and really rounds out the game.

Most cards don’t have a lot of text or effects beyond their base function, aside from event cards and “Play Immediately” cards, which I really appreciated. It keeps things simple to track, and the main thing to manage is resources, whether for building stronger cards or boosting attack and defence. When events call for a fight, it’s simple to resolve too, just compare attack and defence points. That lack of clutter makes this a great pick for introducing new players to deck building without extra rules to juggle.

All three plays were enjoyable. This was a game I’d never even heard of before, and I’m glad I got the chance to put it on the table and try it out. I’ll definitely be bringing it to the group to see how it plays with others.

My Rating

Note: 7/10

There are other deck builders I enjoy more, like Ascension, Legendary Encounters: Alien, and Harry Potter: Hogwarts Battle. Those are more complete and complex games. But Era of Kingdoms is a lovely way to introduce new players to deck building, and it’s worth it for the illustrations alone.

Final Thoughts

It’s still an enjoyable game that deserves to be better known. It’s a solid option for anyone who enjoys lite deck building with beautiful illustrations.

Your Turn

Have you played Era of Kingdoms, or do you have another lite deck builder with gorgeous art that deserves more love? Come share them on Mastodon and *Facebook

Related Links

  • Era of Kingdoms on BoardGameGeek
  • KC Games Website

  • How to Play ERA OF KINGDOMS w/ a Solo Playthrough - Solo Playthrough by Dale the Casual Gamer
  • Era of Kingdoms - Overview - Game overview by Board Game Coffee

item.title: April 2026 Plays
item.description:
Hello everyone!

What a month April was! I played a lot, I laughed a lot, and I discovered some real gems along the way. 32 plays over 17 different games, more than double my March count of 15. That says it all, really. 😊

April 2026 by the Numbers

  • 32 plays (vs. 15 in March, more than double!)
  • 17 different games
  • 10 new-to-me games
  • Most played: Onirim (6 plays)

Onirim

Onirim is not new to me. I’ve owned it for a few years now and I keep coming back to it. It’s part of the Oniverse, a collection of small-box games designed for solo or two players, all set in the same dream world. Eight games in the series so far, and while they all share the same universe, each one feels genuinely different from the others. Onirim was my entry point into the Oniverse and it holds a special place in my heart. It reminds me of the solitaire card games I used to play as a kid. The goal is to escape the labyrinth by finding the eight exit doors, using only cards, but be careful not to cross paths with a nightmare! It’s quick, tense in the best possible way, and an absolute must-have for solo players. I’ll dedicate a full review to it one day. It deserves one.

Red Rising

Red Rising was technically already in my collection, but this month was the first time I actually sat down to play it, and it won me over quickly. I lost only once out of four plays, but the win/loss count almost misses the point: what kept me coming back was how differently each game played out. The combo mechanics between the different castes are the heart of this game, and there are so many ways to build a hand that each play genuinely felt like a different puzzle to solve. The solo mode is quick to set up and easy to run, but don’t let that fool you. It’s genuinely hard to beat. I already have a full review written and ready to post, so I won’t say too much more here. Keep an eye out. It deserves its own spotlight!

It’s a Wonderful World

I honestly can’t fully explain the pull this game has on me. With more than 25 plays under my belt, solo and at two players, you’d think the magic would wear off. It hasn’t. This month I came back to it in solo mode and, well, I lost. But even losing felt satisfying.

The balance between building an efficient production engine and building a scoring engine is just perfect. You can have a smooth game where resources flow freely and cards go down easily, and still lose because none of them actually scored you points. It’s that tension that keeps me coming back. The theme doesn’t hit you over the head, but the artwork is lovely. More plays incoming for sure.

Last Will

Last Will is a game I really love, but since it’s a multiplayer-only experience, I hadn’t had the chance to play it in a while. That changed this month, thanks to a wonderful new development: I’ve started joining the monthly and weekly meetings of Legiao dos Jogos. What an amazing group of people! It’s been such a joy to bring some of my favourite games to the table, and to discover new ones alongside them.

So, Last Will finally hit the table again, and at four players no less. The premise is wonderfully absurd: instead of trying to become the richest player, you have to spend all your money. Sounds easy? It really isn’t. The game is beautifully designed for its theme, the artwork is spot on, and playing it at four created exactly the kind of chaos and laughter I was hoping for. If spending money is your thing, this game is absolutely for you. 😄

Other Notable Games

Multiplayer discoveries with Legião dos Jogos

Being part of the group also meant discovering, or rediscovering, some great lighter games. I got to play The Gang, The Game, Codenames, Take 5, and Escape: The Curse of the Temple, and they all delivered fun in their own way.

Escape: The Curse of the Temple was my favourite of the bunch. At four players it’s pure glorious chaos: everyone rolling dice at the same time, shouting across the table to coordinate. It’s genuinely one of those experiences where you’re nearly screaming just to be heard, and somehow that makes it even better. If you enjoy real-time games where the table turns into beautiful pandemonium, this one is for you.

Codenames we played at eight, which in my opinion was a bit too many. I’ve played Codenames Harry Potter at two players before, and I think the sweet spot is around six. That gives you two people giving clues, one per team, and two players on each team discussing the hints and making guesses together. At three per team, some people inevitably get less involved, maybe out of shyness or just because the discussion gets harder to follow. At eight it felt a little crowded for me. Fun either way, but six feels like the right balance.

Solo new-to-me games

On the solo front, I explored five new games this month: Era of Kingdoms, Outlive, Side Quest: 7th Sea, Fromage, and Paper Tales.

Era of Kingdoms was a genuine surprise. I had never heard of it before, and it turned out to be a really enjoyable tableau building, deck building, and hand management game. The atmosphere is a bit dark, which suits the theme well. My only small complaint is that some of the symbols could be a bit bigger. For a game that came completely out of nowhere for me, I would absolutely recommend it.

Outlive was a game I had been wanting to play for a long time. I almost got to it last year, but then I realised I needed the Underwater expansion to unlock the solo mode, so the experience had to wait. It was worth it. I love the survival theme, and the worker placement twist is clever: you never retrieve your workers from the board, you can only move them. It forces you to think carefully about placement at every step. The automa is pleasant to manage, and as a collector’s edition owner, I can confirm the components are just stunning.

SideQuest: 7th Sea is an escape room game from the SideQuest series by Board & Dice. The puzzles in the first part of the game were well-balanced and satisfying. The second part was trickier. I struggled at times to figure out what I was supposed to do. I own two more games from the series, so it’ll be interesting to see if that difficulty curve feels the same across them.

Fromage immediately charmed me. The theme is exactly what it sounds like: you’re making cheese. The worker placement mechanic is wonderfully on theme too. The more elaborate the cheese you’re making, the longer your workers are tied up in the affinage process. It’s clever, it’s thematic, and the components are just delightful, including that cheese board-shaped board! I only played solo this time, but I’m already curious to try it at two or three players.

Paper Tales left me with mixed feelings, though I suspect that’s partly on me. I think I made some resource management mistakes on my first play. The core idea is interesting: you have limited tableau space, and you’ll place your workers and fighters to defeat the solo king. What I found particularly charming is the ageing mechanic. Your characters grow old and eventually die, which adds a lovely layer of bittersweet planning. I need a few more plays before I can say anything definitive, but the concept is good and I want to give it a fair chance.

Games I Keep Coming Back To

Dice Throne Adventure

I’ve mentioned this one in previous monthly reviews, and here I am again. I’m still working my way through the campaign in solo, and I’m now into the fourth scenario. The pattern has become something of a ritual: I almost always lose the first attempt at each new scenario, except for the third one, which I beat on my very first try. Very proud of that! The fourth scenario has already beaten me once, so I’ll be going back in for another try. The campaign is funny, addictive, and just the right amount of punishing.

Ancient Knowledge

Ancient Knowledge is another game that requires the expansion to play solo, in this case the Heritage expansion. I’ve played it before but April reminded me that I still haven’t cracked the winning formula. I lost again, and I have a feeling I’m simply forgetting the recipe between plays! Fair warning: the cards carry a lot of text, so if that puts you off, this one probably isn’t for you. I do like the game though, and one of these days I’ll figure out how to actually win it. 😅

Viticulture

Have I mentioned that I love Viticulture? Because I really love Viticulture. Solo, every single point counts. One wrong decision and the win slips away. I’m genuinely curious to explore the Tuscany and Bordeaux expansions at some point. Something to look forward to.

Looking Ahead

May is looking exciting! My main goal is to finally finish the Dice Throne Adventure campaign. The fifth scenario still owes me a win. Beyond that, I’m feeling the pull of Minos, Unconscious Mind, and Luthier. I don’t know which one will make it to the table first, but I have a feeling at least one of them won’t wait much longer.

What About You?

What a month it’s been! New groups, new games, old favourites. April had it all. Are any of these games on your radar? Have you played any of them? Come share your thoughts on Mastodon.
